title: Hidden from the wise (Luke 10:21–24)
hook: Jesus rejoices that simple people understand

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy sent out two by two. Your line was peace be to this house. Did you carry peace through a door? Day five hundred forty.

The Gospels show Jesus weeping, sighing, angry at injustice, tired enough to sleep through a storm. They seldom say outright that he was joyful. That's what makes today's four verses stand out. The seventy have just come back, buzzing with stories, and Jesus has told them: rejoice that your names are written in heaven. And then Luke says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit." The Greek verb is stronger than the English. It's the word for exulting, being overjoyed, the same family of words Mary used when she sang that her spirit rejoiced in God. What could make him that happy? Not who you'd expect.

Here's what he says, in the King James words: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight." Babes, in Greek nepioi, means little children, infants. Not the experts. Not the people with the best schooling or the highest positions. Luke never tells us who the seventy were, only that they were sent out with no purse and no bag, and they've just seen what many learned people missed. Jesus isn't against learning. Luke himself opens his Gospel saying he investigated everything carefully. The point is about the door you come in by. Some things you don't grasp by being clever. You grasp them the way a child does: by trusting, by receiving, by not pretending you already know. The wise and prudent, the people who are sure they understand, can find the door closed precisely because they're sure. Then Jesus turns to his disciples privately: "Blessed are the eyes which see the things that ye see: For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them." Kings. Prophets. Isaiah, David, all the great names. They longed to see this, and the ones who got to see it are a group of ordinary people from Galilee. It's a strange, warm reversal, and it fits Luke's whole Gospel: the shepherds before the priests, the widow before the rich, the child set beside him. The ones who receive are the ones who know they need to.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE EYES WHICH SEE THE THINGS THAT YE SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone the world wouldn't call an expert. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who've taught you the most important things, not from a stage, but by how they lived. A grandmother who prayed while she cooked. A child who forgave quickly. A coworker with no title who always knew the right thing to do. Someone with a disability, or a hard life, who sees what others miss. Let one face come. What did they understand that cleverness couldn't teach? Then think of someone you'll meet today whom you might overlook as a teacher. Decide to listen to them as if they knew something you don't. If you pray, you can give thanks for your unexpected teachers. If you don't, simply honor them. The bell holds the time.
Nepioi, Greek for little children, infants: Jesus rejoices that what the clever missed has been revealed to little children, ordinary people who simply received it.
Your line: revealed to babes. Today, ask one person you'd normally overlook what they think, and really listen to the answer. Day five hundred forty.

howItsDone: Many Christians treasure Luke 10:21 as a reminder that faith is open to everyone, and teachers of prayer across traditions often speak of receiving God like a child.

myth: the Gospels seldom say outright that Jesus rejoiced
Luke 10:21 is one of the few places.
he's speaking of how things are received: like a child, trusting, not pretending to know.
Jesus said kings and prophets had longed to see what the disciples saw

fork.setup: your followers, ordinary people sent out with no purse and no bag, have just understood what experts missed. how do you respond?
options: tell them not to get proud.
rejoice, and thank the Father for revealing it to little children.
send them to study with the experts.
fork.reveal: Jesus rejoices in spirit and thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to babes.

original.note: Greek: little children, infants. the "babes" to whom these things are revealed.

trapdoor: what you thought: smart people can't understand God.
what it means: what matters most is received like a child receives, and those who are sure they already know can miss it.
what a scholar hears: "rejoiced" is agalliao, to exult, the same verb family as Mary's "my spirit hath rejoiced" in Luke 1:47.

notes: 'The Gospels seldom say outright that he was joyful': agalliao for Jesus appears only here; John 11:15 has 'I am glad' (chairo). Confirm wording.
Luke 1:47 uses egalliasen (agalliao), the same verb as 10:21. Confirm.
Some manuscripts read 'rejoiced in the Holy Spirit' in 10:21.
The voice mentions Jesus 'weeping' (Luke 19:41) and 'tired enough to sleep through a storm' (Luke 8:23).
Audit (y2 10% sample): removed the unsourced claim that the seventy were 'fishermen and farmers' (Luke 10 does not say who they were); teach and fork setup now describe them from Luke 10:4.
